# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-31 (Extended v206)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to autumn Year 8. Primary Paris locations: Rue Plumet, Place de la Bastille, Prison Chargemagne, Rue de l'Homme Armé No. 6, Champ-de-Mars, Halles district, Rue du Pont-aux-Choux, Rue de Thorigny, Marché Saint-Jean, Rue des Billettes, Rue Saint-Denis, Rue de la Chanvrerie, Rue de la Petite-Truanderie, Rue Mondétour, Pointe Saint-Eustache, Rue du Cygne, Rue des Prêcheurs, Rue Blomet, Rue de Rivoli, Place Louis XV, Champs-Élysées, Esplanade, bridge of Invalides, Hôtel des Princes, Hôtel Meurice, Rue Saint-Honoré, Passage Delorme, Place du Palais-Royal, Rue de Béthisy, Rue des Bourdonnais, Rue de la Poterie, Rue du Contrat-Social, Marché-aux-Poirées, Rue de Babylone, Rue du Chaume, Rue des Vieilles-Haudriettes, Royal Printing Establishment, Luxembourg Garden, Rue de Pontoise, Rue Polonceau, Café Corinthe, Rue de l'Étoile, Rue Saint-Louis, Rue du Temple, Rue Vieille-du-Temple, Rue Notre-Dame de Nazareth, Rue Folie-Méricourt, Quai aux Fleurs, Rue du Petit-Musc, Rue du Normandie, Rue Pont-Aux-Biches, Rue des Marais, Faubourg Saint-Martin, Rue Notre Dame des-Victoires, Faubourg Montmartre, Rue Grange-Batelière, Rue Jacob, Rue de Tournon, Pont au Change, Pont-Neuf, Sewer des Halles, Seine, Sainte-Avoye sewer, Rue Michel-le-Comte, sewer of the Louvre, Montmartre sewer, Rue du Cadran, belt sewer, Saint-Merry, Quay, Passy, Pont de Jéna, Bercy, Amelot sewer, Isle Louviers, Quartier Popincourt, Ménilmontant, Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire, Carrefour Boucherat, Corridor Saint-Louis, Saint-Gilles gut, Saint-Sebastian gallery, Arsenal, Faubourg Saint-Honoré, Quartier Saint-Georges, Quartier des Martyrs, gallery des Martyrs, Beautreillis sewer, Quai des Ormes, Grève, Place du Châtelet, Pont Notre-Dame, Quai de la Mégisserie. English locations: Kelmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Dungate, Ravenmere, Staveford, Wilwick, Salcombe, Dunstead, Wilholt, Torton, Quenford, Pontoise, Stenenridge, Gulhaven, Barrière d'Enfer, Esplanade de l'Observatoire, Yarlby, Gagny, Lagny, Jondrette's garret, Montfermeil.

## English Subplot Summary

**Rumored claims**: Yera Stenworth confided fire at Dunstead granary set deliberately (autumn Year 7). Fenelle Lindmere and Marald revealed Stenson family owed blood debt to Stenenridge family. Ferald Stenworth confided same. In letter Ismira Stenson burned, Elra revealed deed to Kelmere pastures forged. Kassa Brackick whispered Islan Thornmere secretly married Yera Haskick (autumn Year 7). Movie Prydenridge rumored Rorald Lindmere dead of plague.

**Confirmed rumors**: Fire at Dunstead granary set on purpose. Stenenridge mill ledger rewritten after flood.

**Established facts**: Kassa Brackick and Volan Stenworth married at Staveford; Kassa went to Dungate. Taric Corrley quit Staveford for Dungate lodgings. Marald Corrford quit Dunstead for Salcombe; Fenelle followed within month. Ismira Stenson quit Dungate for Elmhaven (winter Year 6). Matho Stenson went to Elmhaven (winter Year 6). Elra Corrford settled in Elmhaven. Havie Prydenridge promised Gadrek Prydenridge to pay old debt to Stenworth family. Gadrek quit milling, took brewery work (autumn Year 7). Kassa Stenson's husband swore to rebuild fallen wall at Ostcombe. Fenelle found Elmhaven work, moved there (summer Year 7); Marald followed within month. Zavus Prydenridge apprenticed anew, became ferryman (summer Year 7). Islan Thornmere quit Ostcombe for Dungate lodgings (autumn Year 7). Vesmira Thornmere went to Dungate (autumn Year 7). Movie Prydenridge married only son of Luena Stenenridge at Ostcombe; couple lived there thereafter. Kassa Stenson kept promise to Taric Corrley: wall at Yarlby rebuilt by harvest. Havie and Isric Thornmere wed at Ostcombe with half parish present; lived there thereafter. Matho Stenson moved from Elmhaven to Staveford (winter Year 7). Fenelle followed Marald to Ravenmere within month. Elra Corrford rode out of Elmhaven; by next market day living in Gulhaven. Red Ismira went along to live in Staveford. Islan Thornmere died of old age, quietly in sleep at Dungate. Gadrek Prydenridge married eldest daughter of Lura Haskick in chapel at Ostcombe; couple lived in Ostcombe from then on. Luvie Prydenridge and Semor wed at Ostcombe. Luena Stenenridge sent copper chalice by carrier to Yera Stenworth, who received it safely. In letter Gadrek burned, revealed old abbey at Gulhaven hides second cellar. Yera Haskick swore to Nerine Prydenridge to repair roof of chapel at Kelmere, and shook on it. Havie Prydenridge never kept promise made to Gadrek Prydenridge (pay old debt owed to Stenworth family); matter abandoned.

**Solemn promises**: Elra gave Matho solemn promise to plant orchard on slope above Gulhaven. Pelia gave Fenelle solemn promise to plant orchard on slope above Salcombe (summer Year 7). Movie swore to Nerine to plant orchard on slope above Wilholt, shook on it (autumn Year 7).

**New births and marriages (Spring Year 7)**: Rinelle Corrley and Kadrek Brackick had son Movus Brackick (Wilholt). Nerine Prydenridge and Lurald Stenworth wed at Ostcombe, had son Istho Stenworth (Ostcombe). Wenelle Lindmere and Rovus Prydenridge had son Febin Prydenridge (Kelmere). Bremira Corrford and Zavus Prydenridge married at Dunstead. Ferald and Zalis Corrley wed at Dunstead (summer Year 7).

**Broken faith**: Rorald Lindmere broke faith with Kassa Stenson—promised work never begun.

**Property transfers**: Kassa Brackick won bone compass from Volan Stenworth at cards, fairly, kept it. Kassa Brackick gave amber map to Volan Stenworth (summer Year 8). **Kassa Brackick gave bone compass to Ismira (autumn Year 8).**

**Recent work changes (autumn Year 8)**: Luvie Prydenridge gave up weaving, took work as chandler.

**Recent regretted purchases**: Yera Haskick, Ilrald, Ferald Stenworth, Volan Stenworth, Rimor Corrford each bought ribbon at stall and regretted it.

**Recent activities**: Luvie fell asleep in chair before fire caught. Isvie Stenworth fell asleep in chair before fire had caught. Isric spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight. Yera Haskick and Havie asked "Will it rain?" receiving only shrug from Yera. Rain threatened since morning but held off; children chased hoop down lane shrieking. Someone chalked crooked sun on wall of forge. Gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps. Baker's boy was late; line at oven grew long. Cart loaded with turnips creaked past well. Dog barked at nothing then went quiet. Zavus Prydenridge told Zalis "You look tired"; Zalis did not deny it. Volan and Kassa talked of nothing much—weather, harvest, lame horse. Volan remarked river was up; Matho Stenson said it always was in spring. Matho hummed tune from childhood while scrubbing step. Ismira walked long way round to avoid muddy square in Staveford hill farms. Bell for vespers rang thinly across roofs. Light went early as it did that time of year.

**Rumor (autumn Year 8)**: Bremira told everyone at inn that Rovus Prydenridge drowned crossing estuary, though no body was ever seen.

## Marius and Cosette's Romance and Marriage

**Recognition and love**: Cosette acknowledged never forgot Marius, always loved him. Beginning autumn Year 5, Marius came every evening. **Confessions (spring Year 6)**: Marius told Cosette—orphan, name Marius Pontmercy, lawyer, father colonel and hero. Cosette told Marius—brought up at Petit-Picpus convent, mother dead, father M. Fauchelevent. **Éponine's death (evening 24th June)**: Éponine revealed she led Marius to barricade. Gave Marius letter from Cosette before dying. **Cosette's letter content**: Marriage impossible; grandfather refuses; no fortune; hastened to him, he gone; kept promise given; dies; loves him. **Marius joins barricade (evening 24th June)**: Upon learning Valjean plans England departure in one week, arranged meeting 26th June. Same evening, rushed to barricade. **Barricade combat (6th June)**: Witnessed M. Mabeuf's death, Bahorel killed; flung self into conflict. Saved Gavroche with first shot. **Marius's wound (6th June)**: Shot broke collar bone; felt fainting and falling. Vigorous hand seized him before consciousness vanished.

**Marius's medical condition and recovery (Chapters 27-30)**: Bullet deadened by pocket-book, turned aside, made tour of ribs with hideous laceration, not dangerous. Long underground journey dislocated broken collar-bone seriously. Arms slashed with sabre cuts. Head fairly covered with cuts. Grave symptom: swoons caused by wounds; might cause brain damage. Exhausted by hemorrhage. **7 September (four months after retrieval)**: Doctor declared Marius would recover. Convalescence began. Forced to remain two months more on long chair due to collar-bone fracture. One wound type will not close, prolongs dressings indefinitely. This long illness saved him from all pursuit—six months extinguishes public wrath. Gisquet order outraged public opinion and King; wounded protected; councils of war did not dare trouble anyone. Marius left in peace.

**M. Gillenormand's devotion and later conflict (Chapter 30-31)**: Passed through anguish then ecstasy. Had big armchair carried to Marius' bedside; required daughter to take finest linen for compresses. Present at all wound dressings. At each improvement, grandfather raved with joy. Marius became master of house; abdication in grandfather's joy. In state of joy, grandfather most venerable of children. Stepped behind to smile lest he might fatigue. White locks added gentle majesty to gay radiance. **However, as Marius regained health and reflected on past, Colonel Pontmercy and Gillenormand's injustice to father came between them. Marius grew cold; old man gently pained. Gillenormand observed that Marius, since brought back and regained consciousness, had not once called him father; avoided both "father" and "monsieur" by turning phrases. Obvious crisis approaching.** Marius tested ground (Chapter 30): Speaking severely of Convention, declared "The men of '93 were giants." Gillenormand held peace remainder of day. Another morning, Gillenormand suggested eating meat for convalescence; Marius was overwhelmed with emotions. **When Marius called grandfather "father" three times, Gillenormand agreed to bring Cosette to him.** While relating André Chénier poem ending, Gillenormand was clutched by his own phrase about Chénier being guillotined; unable to finish or retract, rushed from bedroom, found Basque in anteroom, seized him by collar, shouted in fury: "By the hundred thousand Javottes of the devil, those ruffians did assassinate him!"

**Marriage arrangement and Cosette's arrival (Chapter 31)**: Cosette was intoxicated, delighted, frightened, in heaven; thoroughly alarmed by happiness. Stammered pale yet flushed; wanted to fling herself into Marius' arms, dared not. Ashamed of loving before others. Aunt Gillenormand looked on in amazement—stupid eye of poor innocent fifty-seven years old; life which had been failure gazing at triumph of love. Porter nearly recognized Fauchelevent from night of 7th June when he arrived tattered, muddy, hideous, carrying fainting Marius; porter's scent aroused but did not identify him. Cosette learned she was not daughter of old man she called father; he was merely kinsman; another Fauchelevent was her real father. At this moment, revelation cast but slight shadow, faint cloud; she was so full of joy cloud did not last long. She had Marius. Young man arrived, old man was effaced; such is life. Cosette happy as angels, enthusiastic over Father Gillenormand.

**Gillenormand's remarks on marriage and gifts (Chapter 31)**: Called Cosette "exquisite darling," "masterpiece," said she born Marquise, only becoming Baroness is comedown. Warned of misfortune: more than half his possessions swallowed in annuity; after his death (score of years hence), they will have nothing. Called Marius "that devil" who ferreted millionaire grisette in tree of dreams. Said students find studentesses with six hundred thousand francs. Overwhelmed Cosette with gallant compliments and presents. Gave her robe of Binche guipure descended from his own grandmother. Rifled respectable chests of drawers in Coromandel lacquer, violated pot-bellied drawers of all his wives, mistresses, grandmothers. Lavished Pekins, damasks, lampas, painted moires, robes of shot gros de Tours, India kerchiefs embroidered in gold, dauphines, Genoa and Alençon point lace, parures in antique goldsmith's work, ivory bon-bon boxes, gewgaws and ribbons on Cosette. Furnished chamber with multitude of elegant trifles. Had ceiling and walls hung with extraordinary stuff, buttercup-colored satin ground covered with velvet auricula blossoms—claimed same stuff draped bed of Duchesse d'Anville at la Roche-Guyon. Set little figure in Saxe porcelain on chimney-piece, carrying muff against nude stomach.

**Cosette's dowry (Chapter 31)**: Five hundred and eighty thousand francs constituted legacy bequeathed to Cosette by dead person desiring to remain unknown. Original legacy consisted of five hundred and ninety-four thousand francs; ten thousand expended on education of Mademoiselle Euphrasie, five thousand paid to convent. Legacy deposited in third party's hands, to be turned over to Cosette at majority or marriage date. Very acceptable sum—half million. Some peculiarities existed but not noticed; one interested party had eyes blindfolded by love, others by six hundred thousand francs. Cosette dreamed of happiness without limit clothed in satin and velvet; wedding basket seemed upheld by seraphim; soul flew out into azure depths with wings of Mechlin lace.

**Aunt Gillenormand's indifference (Chapter 31)**: Surveyed all this with imperturbable placidity. Within last five or six months experienced: Marius returned, brought back bleeding, brought back from barricade, dead, then living, reconciled, betrothed, wedding poor girl, wedding millionairess. Six hundred thousand francs her last surprise. Then indifference of girl taking first communion returned to her. Went regularly to service, told beads, read euchology, mumbled _Aves_ in one corner while "I love you" whispered in other. Beheld Marius and Cosette vaguely, like two shadows. Shadow was herself. In state of inert asceticism, soul neutralized by torpor, stranger to business of living, received no impressions human or pleasant or painful except earthquakes and catastrophes—corresponds to cold in head; smells nothing of life, neither bad nor good odor.

**Marius's doubts about past (Chapter 31)**: Surrounded M. Fauchelevent with mute questions; benevolent and cold to him. Moments when doubts as to own recollections occurred. Void in memory, black spot, abyss excavated by four months of agony; many things lost therein. Questioned whether really fact he saw M. Fauchelevent at barricade—serious, calm man. Wondered whether he himself was actually same man. Poor man become rich; abandoned had family; despairing to marry Cosette. Felt he traversed tomb, entered black and emerged white; others remained therein. Beings of past, returned and present, formed circle, overshadowed him; thought of Cosette recovered serenity; nothing less than felicity could suffice to efface catastrophe. Hesitated to believe Fauchelevent of barricade same as this Fauchelevent in flesh and blood, sitting gravely beside Cosette. First was probably nightmare occasioned by delirium hours. Natures of both men rigid; no question from Marius to M. Fauchelevent was possible. Such idea had not occurred to him.

**Thénardier family's fate (Chapter 31)**: None of Marius's agents succeeded discovering trace of Thénardier. Obliteration appeared complete. Madame Thénardier died in prison pending trial. Thénardier and daughter Azelma, only two remaining of lamentable group, plunged back into gloom. Gulf of social unknown silently closed above those beings. On surface not visible so much as quiver, trembling, obscure concentric circles announcing something fallen in. Affair remained obscure. Bench of Assizes obliged to content themselves with two subordinates: Panchaud, alias Printanier, alias Bigrenaille, and Demi-Liard, alias Deux-Milliards, inconsistently condemned after hearing of both sides to ten years in galleys. Hard labor for life pronounced against escaped and contumacious accomplices.

**Mystery of Valjean's rescue agent (Chapter 31)**: Marius's agent who saved him gave no sign of life. His disinterestedness no less tremendous than devotion. Why had not that man appeared again? Perhaps above compensation, but no one above gratitude. Was he dead? What sort of face had he? No one could tell Marius this.

## Javert's Moral Crisis and Death (Chapter 30)

**Change in consciousness**: Up to day of Valjean's emergence, Javert borrowed from Napoleon only resolution and certainty. Now whole person slow and sombre, stamped with anxiety. Brain so limpid in blindness lost transparency; crystal clouded. Duty divided within conscience.

**Encounter at Seine**: When unexpectedly encountered Valjean on banks of Seine, beheld two paths, both equally straight, both contrary. Which was true?

**Valjean's transformation in Javert's perception**: Valjean disconcerted him. All axioms crumbled. Valjean's generosity crushed him. Facts formerly treated as lies recurred as realities. M. Madeleine reappeared behind Jean Valjean; two figures superposed, forming one venerable image. Something terrible penetrated soul—admiration for convict. Respect for galley-slave—possible? Shuddered, could not escape. Confess sublimity of wretch. Odious.

**Moral transformation perceived**: Benevolent malefactor, merciful, gentle, helpful, clement, convict returning good for evil, giving pardon for hatred, preferring pity to vengeance, preferring to ruin himself rather than ruin enemy. Kneeling on heights of virtue, more nearly akin to angel than man. Javert constrained to admit monster existed.

**Loss of certainty**: Supreme anguish was loss of certainty. Felt uprooted. Code no longer anything but stump in hand. Had to deal with scruples of unknown species. Sentimental revelation entirely distinct from legal affirmation, his only standard hitherto. Whole order of unexpected facts cropped up, subjugated him. New world dawning: kindness accepted and repaid, devotion, mercy, indulgence, respect for persons, no more definitive condemnation, possibility of tear in eye of law, no one knows what justice according to God, running inverse to justice according to men. Perceived terrible rising of unknown moral sun; horrified and dazzled. Owl forced to gaze of eagle.

**Superior authority consciousness and rift**: This new chief, God, became unexpectedly conscious of; felt embarrassed by him. Unforeseen presence threw off bearings. Could not return Valjean to Rue de l'Homme Armé. Could not.

**Suicide (evening, Place du Châtelet)**: Traversed Place du Châtelet diagonally, regained quay, returned to point abandoned quarter hour previously. Darkness complete, sepulchral moment following midnight. Ceiling of clouds concealed stars. Streets and quays deserted. Street lantern reddened margin of quay. Bridges lay shapeless in mist. River could not be seen; only foam audible. In dizzy depth, gleam of light appeared, undulated vaguely. Wall abrupt, mingled with vapors, produced effect of escarpment of infinite. Fierce breath rose from abyss. Flood divined rather than perceived, tragic whispering of waves, melancholy vastness of arches of bridge, imaginable fall into gloomy void—all shadow full of horror. Remained motionless several minutes gazing at opening of shadow. Took off hat, placed it on edge of quay. Tall black figure appeared erect upon parapet, bent over towards Seine, drew self up, fell straight down into shadows; dull splash followed; shadow alone in secret of convulsions of obscure form disappeared beneath water. **Javert is dead (suicide by drowning).**

**Jean Valjean's knowledge**: Jean Valjean knew he was delivered from Javert. Story verified in _Moniteur_: police inspector named Javert found drowned under boat belonging to laundresses, between Pont au Change and Pont-Neuf. Writing left by this man, otherwise irreproachable and highly esteemed by superiors, pointed to fit of mental aberration and suicide. Valjean concluded: since Javert left him at liberty once having got him in power, he must have been already mad.

## Other Events (Chapter 30)

**Boulatruelle**: Escaped neatly from Jondrette's garret with other ruffians; drunkenness was salvation. Authorities never made out whether he was robber or robbed. Nolle prosequi set him at liberty. Returned to road from Gagny to Lagny, making broken stone under administrative supervision. One morning before daybreak, caught sight of man whose back alone he saw; shape of shoulders not entirely unfamiliar. Man just arrived on foot. Had walked all night from Paris. Compassed hundred strides before day broke. Footprints in sand, weeds trodden down, heather crushed, young branches bent and straightening pointed out track. Followed it, then lost it. Plunged deeper into woods, came to eminence. Beech-tree of great size stood close at hand; climbed as high as able. Man entered open glade at considerable distance, masked by large trees. Glade Boulatruelle knew—near large pile of porous stones, ailing chestnut-tree bandaged with sheet of zinc nailed directly upon bark. This glade formerly called Blaru-bottom. By beaten paths required quarter hour; in bee-line through underbrush, dense, thorny, full half hour necessary. Man made better time than expected; Boulatruelle's pursuit difficult.
